items.title: Identity Theft Enforcement and Protection Act — notification following breach of security of computerized data
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §521.053(c), any person who maintains computerized data that includes sensitive personal information not owned by that person must notify the owner or license holder of the information of any breach of system security immediately after discovering the breach, if the information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify the data owner: 'immediately after discovering' the breach (§521.053(c))

Owner/licensee duty to notify affected individuals: 'without unreasonable delay and in each case not later than the 60th day after the date on which the person determines that the breach occurred' (§521.053(b))
Notify the Texas Attorney General 'as soon as practicable and not later than the 30th day' after determining the breach occurred, if the breach involves at least 250 Texas residents (§521.053(i))
items.notice_deadline: Vendor to owner: 'immediately after discovering the breach.' Owner to individuals: 'without unreasonable delay and in each case not later than the 60th day after the date on which the person determines that the breach occurred.'
items.regulator_notice: Texas Attorney General, not later than the 30th day after determining the breach occurred, if the breach involves at least 250 Texas residents (§521.053(i))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Sensitive personal information' (§521.002(a)(2)) includes name/initials + SSN, driver's license/govt ID, or financial account number with access code; or health information identifying an individual's physical/mental health condition, health care, or payment for health care.
items.penalties: Civil penalty $2,000–$50,000 per violation; additional penalty up to $100 per affected person per day of delay in required notice, capped at $250,000 per breach (§521.151)

items.title: Texas Student Privacy Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to 'operators' — operators of a website, online service, online application, or mobile application who have actual knowledge that the product is used primarily for a school purpose and was designed and marketed for a school purpose. Operators are restricted from targeted advertising based on student data, creating non-school-purpose student profiles, and selling/renting covered student information.
key_obligations: No targeted advertising based on student information or persistent identifiers acquired through school-purpose use
No creating student profiles from collected data except for school purposes
No selling or renting covered student information (narrow exceptions for acquisitions and national assessment providers with parental consent)
Disclosure permitted only for legitimate school purposes, legal/regulatory compliance, safety/security, judicial process, or school-contracted services with confidentiality requirements
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Covered information' is personally identifiable information not publicly available, created by/provided to an operator by a student, parent, or school employee for a school purpose, or gathered by the operator through the service.
items.uncertainty: Penalty/enforcement provision for this subchapter was not independently located this session; not stated in the summarized source.

items.title: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (TDPSA)
items.applies_to_vendor: As a 'processor' (§541.001(23), a person that processes personal data on behalf of a controller), LOVELEEDAY must follow controller instructions, assist with consumer-rights requests and data security, and enter into a written contract (§541.104) covering processing instructions, nature/purpose, data types, duration, confidentiality of personnel, deletion/return of data, audit cooperation, and flow-down subcontractor obligations.
key_obligations: Applies to entities conducting business in Texas or targeting Texas residents that process/sell personal data and are not SBA-classified small businesses; small businesses remain subject to §541.107 (consent before selling sensitive data)
Exempt: state agencies/political subdivisions, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA-covered entities, nonprofits, institutions of higher education, electric utilities

Processor-controller contracts required under §541.104(b): processing instructions/nature/purpose/data types/duration, confidentiality duty for personnel, deletion/return obligations, audit cooperation, and written subcontractor agreements with equivalent obligations
Enforcement is AG-exclusive with no private right of action (§541.151, §541.156); 30-day cure notice required before suit (§541.154)
items.penalties: Civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation after the cure period expires or a cure commitment is breached (§541.155); AG may also recover attorney's fees and investigative expenses
items.effective_or_amended: Effective July 1, 2024; §541.104 amended effective January 1, 2026 (Acts 2025, 89th Leg., Ch. 1174, H.B. 149) to add AI system references

items.title: Protection of Personal Information Act — disclosure of system security breach
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §13-44-202(3)(a), a person who maintains computerized data that includes personal information the person does not own or license shall notify and cooperate with the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of system security immediately following the person's discovery of the breach if misuse of the personal information occurs or is reasonably likely to occur; cooperation includes sharing information relevant to the breach.
key_obligations: Owner/licensee must conduct a good-faith, reasonable, and prompt investigation on becoming aware of a breach (§13-44-202(1)(a))
If investigation shows misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, notify each affected Utah resident 'in the most expedient time possible without unreasonable delay' (§13-44-202(1)(b), (2))
If misuse affects 500+ Utah residents, also notify the Office of the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center (§13-44-202(1)(c))
If misuse affects 1,000+ Utah residents, also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies (§13-44-202(1)(d))
No private right of action; AG may enforce (per secondary sources — not located in the text fetched this session)
items.notice_deadline: 'in the most expedient time possible without unreasonable delay,' after determining scope of breach and restoring reasonable system integrity
items.regulator_notice: Utah AG and Utah Cyber Center, if misuse relates to 500 or more Utah residents; no fixed day count given, notice required 'to the extent the information is known or available at the time the person provides the notification'
items.uncertainty: Could not independently confirm a specific civil-penalty dollar amount for this section this session (private-right-of-action bar and AG enforcement are reported by secondary sources but not directly re-verified against the enforcement section text).

items.title: Student Privacy and Data Protection — Third-party contractors
items.applies_to_vendor: A third-party contractor receiving personally identifiable student data under a contract with an education entity must use it strictly for the contracted product/service, may not sell student data, may not collect/use/share data inconsistently with the contract, and may not use student data for targeted advertising (§53E-9-309(1), (6)). Contracts must include data-handling restrictions, sharing limits, deletion provisions, audit rights, and termination-for-privacy-violation terms with no vendor fee/liability on termination.
key_obligations: No sale of student data (narrow exception for acquisitions/mergers where the successor stays compliant)
No collection/use/sharing inconsistent with the education-entity contract
No targeted advertising using student data
Must return or delete personally identifiable student data at contract completion unless parent/adult student consents to retention

Education entity must terminate the contract (no sooner than 30 days after notice) if the contractor does not remedy a privacy violation within that window; contractor may not charge a fee or assert damages for such termination
items.notice_deadline: Education entity must notify the contractor of a discovered violation within 30 days after discovery, then may terminate no sooner than 30 days after that notice if uncured
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Personally identifiable student data' as used and cross-referenced to FERPA/COPPA protections in the section.

items.title: Utah Consumer Privacy Act (UCPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: As a 'processor' under §13-61-301, LOVELEEDAY must adhere to the controller's instructions and, using appropriate technical/organizational measures, help the controller meet its obligations (including breach notification under §13-44-202). Before processing, processor and controller must have a contract covering processing instructions, nature/purpose, data types, duration, rights/obligations of both parties, personnel confidentiality duty, and flow-down subcontractor obligations.
key_obligations: Applies to controllers/processors conducting business in Utah or targeting Utah residents with ≥$25,000,000 annual revenue AND (≥100,000 consumers' data controlled/processed per year, OR ≥25,000 consumers' data with >50% of gross revenue from data sales) (§13-61-102)

Broad exemptions: government entities, tribes, higher-ed institutions, nonprofits, HIPAA-covered entities/business associates, GLBA financial institutions, FCRA-regulated activity, FERPA data, employment data, and more (§13-61-102(2))
Processor obligations and required contract terms at §13-61-301
Enforcement is AG-exclusive; 30-day cure notice required before an enforcement action, with an express written cure statement (§13-61-402); no private right of action
items.penalties: Up to $7,500 per violation plus actual damages to the consumer, recoverable by the AG after a failed/uncured cure (§13-61-402(3)(d)); proceeds go to the Consumer Privacy Account (capped at $4,000,000, excess reverts to General Fund) (§13-61-403)
items.effective_or_amended: Effective 12/31/2023 (as fetched); a further amended version of §13-61-102 is effective 1/1/2027 per the code's version history
items.uncertainty: A version of §13-61-102 effective 1/1/2027 exists per the code site's version list but was not fetched/compared this session — the applicability thresholds quoted here are the version effective 5/1/2024–1/1/2027.

items.title: Security Breach Notice Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §2435(b)(2), a data collector that maintains computerized data containing personally identifiable information it does not own must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of security immediately following discovery of the breach.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify data owner: 'immediately following discovery of the breach' (§2435(b)(2))
Notify affected consumers 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but not later than 45 days after the discovery or notification' (§2435(b)(1))
Preliminary notice to the Vermont Attorney General or Department of Financial Regulation within 14 business days of discovery (§2435(b)(3)(B)(i))
Follow-up notice to AG/DFR with the number of affected Vermont consumers and a copy of the consumer notice (§2435(b)(3)(C)(i))
items.notice_deadline: Consumers: 'most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but not later than 45 days after the discovery or notification.' Vendor-to-owner: 'immediately following discovery.'
items.regulator_notice: Preliminary notice to Vermont AG/DFR within 14 business days of discovery
items.personal_info_definition_notes: This section incorporates/cross-references a HIPAA-covered-entity definition at §2430(10)(A)(vii); full 'personally identifiable information' definition was not independently re-fetched from §2430 this session.
items.penalties: AG/State's Attorney enforcement authority under §2435(h); secondary sources report civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation, not independently re-verified against statutory text this session.
items.uncertainty: Exact penalty dollar amount ($10,000/violation) is from a secondary source only, not re-confirmed against the statutory enforcement subsection (§2435(h)) this session.

items.title: Vermont student data privacy — operator prohibitions
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to operators of websites/online services/applications used primarily for, and designed and marketed for, PreK–12 school purposes. Operators may not engage in targeted advertising using student data collected for school purposes, may not amass non-school-purpose student profiles, and may not sell, barter, or rent student information.
key_obligations: No targeted advertising on the operator's site/service or elsewhere using data from PreK-12 school use
No building a student profile except for school purposes (does not restrict account info under student/parent/school control)
No sale, barter, or rental of student information (exception for compliant successor entities on acquisition/merger)
Disclosure limited to furtherance of school purposes and other statutory exceptions
Permitted: use of covered information not associated with an identified student to improve/demonstrate effectiveness of the operator's products, including in marketing
items.uncertainty: Penalty/enforcement provision for this specific subchapter was not independently located this session.

items.title: Vermont Data Privacy and Online Surveillance Act (VDPOSA)
items.citation: S.71 (2026), Act 145 — to be codified at 9 V.S.A. chapter 61A, §§ 2415a et seq.
items.applies_to_vendor: As a 'processor' (a person who collects or processes personal data on behalf of a controller or another processor, § 2415a(b)(38)), LOVELEEDAY would be subject to the Act's controller/processor framework once effective. Applies to a person conducting business in Vermont, or producing products/services targeted to Vermont residents, that during the preceding calendar year controlled/processed personal data of ≥35,000 consumers (excluding payment-only data), or controlled/processed sensitive data of ≥3,000 consumers, or derived revenue from selling the personal data of ≥3,000 consumers (§ 2415b(a)).
key_obligations: Applicability thresholds as above (§2415b(a)); consumer-health-data provisions (§2415k) apply more broadly to any person conducting business in or targeting Vermont, regardless of the general thresholds (§2415b(b))
Exemptions include government entities, HIPAA covered entities/business associates that are not hybrid entities, and other listed categories (§2415c)
Enforcement: a violation is deemed a violation of the Vermont Consumer Protection Act (9 V.S.A. ch. 63); AG-exclusive enforcement, no private right of action (§2415j(a))
Mandatory cure period: from January 1, 2028 through June 30, 2029, the AG must issue a notice of violation and allow 60 days to cure before bringing an action (Sec. 3 of the Act)

Consumer health data restrictions (§2415k): no employee/contractor access to consumer health data without a confidentiality duty; no processor access without a compliant processor contract; no geofencing within 1,850 feet of a health facility to target consumers; no sale of consumer health data without consumer consent
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Defines biometric data, consumer health data (incl. gender-affirming and reproductive/sexual health data), genetic data, neural data, precise geolocation data, and sensitive data broadly (§2415a(b)).
items.effective_or_amended: Signed into law June 16, 2026 (after an initial veto on June 8, 2026 was reversed); takes effect January 1, 2028
items.uncertainty: Law is enacted but NOT YET IN EFFECT (effective 1/1/2028) and not yet codified into the numbered Vermont Statutes Online (will be 9 V.S.A. chapter 61A) — source_url is the official bill-status/enacted-text page, not a codified statute page, because none exists yet. Processor-specific contract-term requirements (equivalent to a §2415f/2415g-type section referenced elsewhere in the Act) were not individually pulled from the 58-page enacted text this session; general civil-penalty dollar amount for AG actions under the Consumer Protection Act cross-reference was not independently re-confirmed this session. No general (non-health) breach-notification-style penalty figure is stated in the sections read.

items.title: Breach of personal information notification
items.applies_to_vendor: Section D requires an entity that maintains computerized data that includes personal information that the entity does not own to notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the system without unreasonable delay after discovery of the breach.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify data owner: 'without unreasonable delay' following discovery (§18.2-186.6(D))

Owner/licensee must notify affected residents 'without unreasonable delay' after discovering or being notified of a breach, subject to reasonable delay for scope determination or law-enforcement request (§18.2-186.6(B))
Notify the Attorney General 'without unreasonable delay' when a breach affects more than 1,000 persons at one time (§18.2-186.6(E))
items.notice_deadline: 'without unreasonable delay' (no fixed day count in this section)
items.regulator_notice: Virginia Attorney General, without unreasonable delay, when more than 1,000 persons are affected at one time
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name linked to unencrypted, unredacted SSN, driver's license/ID number, financial account/card number with security code, passport number, or military ID number (§18.2-186.6(A)).
items.penalties: AG may impose civil penalties not to exceed $150,000 per breach or series of similar-nature breaches discovered in a single investigation; individuals may recover direct economic damages (§18.2-186.6(I))

items.title: Vendors providing online school services or school-issued technology
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies directly to vendors ('providers') that contract with a local school division to provide online school services or school-issued technology. Providers must maintain a comprehensive information security program, limit collection/use/sharing of student personal information to consented/contracted purposes, and may not use student data for targeted advertising or sell it.
key_obligations: Maintain a comprehensive information security program reasonably designed to protect security, privacy, confidentiality, and integrity of student personal information

Collect, maintain, use, and share student personal information only with parental consent (for minors) or as authorized in the contract; obtain further consent before deviating from the stated privacy policy
No targeted advertising to students using student personal information
No creating personal profiles except for authorized educational purposes/consent/contract terms
No sale of student data (narrow exception for successor entities via merger/purchase, subject to existing contract obligations)
Delete student personal information within a reasonable time on school request, unless the student/parent objects; wipe school-issued devices before reassignment/disposal
Provide electronic, machine-readable copies of student information on request
No access to location-tracking, audio/visual recording, or monitoring features on school-issued devices except for defined educational/support/legal purposes
items.uncertainty: Penalty/enforcement mechanism for this section was not independently located this session.

items.title: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act (VCDPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: As a 'processor' (§59.1-579), LOVELEEDAY must adhere to controller instructions and, via appropriate technical/organizational measures, help the controller meet its data-security, breach-notification, consumer-rights, and assessment obligations. A binding contract with the controller must set processing instructions, nature/purpose, data types, duration, and party obligations; the processor must impose personnel confidentiality duties, delete/return data on service termination (unless retention is legally required), demonstrate compliance, permit audits/assessments, and bind subcontractors to the same obligations.
key_obligations: Applies to persons conducting business in Virginia or producing products/services targeted to Virginia residents that control/process personal data of ≥100,000 consumers/year, OR control/process data of ≥25,000 consumers AND derive >50% of gross revenue from selling personal data (§59.1-576)
Exempt entities: Commonwealth/political-subdivision bodies, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities/business associates, nonprofits, institutions of higher education (§59.1-576)
Exempt data types: HIPAA PHI, FCRA-regulated data, DPPA data, FERPA records, employment/emergency-contact data (§59.1-576)
Processor contract and duties at §59.1-579
AG-exclusive enforcement; no private right of action; 30-day cure notice required before suit (§59.1-584)
items.penalties: Civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation after failed/uncured 30-day cure period, plus AG's reasonable investigation/preparation expenses including attorney fees (§59.1-584)

items.title: Personal information — Notice of security breaches
items.citation: RCW 19.255.010; definitions at RCW 19.255.005; consumer-protection provision at RCW 19.255.040
items.applies_to_vendor: Under RCW 19.255.010(2), any person or business that maintains or possesses data that may include personal information that it does not own or license shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach immediately following discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify data owner: 'immediately following discovery' (RCW 19.255.010(2))

Owner/licensee must notify affected Washington residents 'in the most expedient time possible, without unreasonable delay, and no more than thirty calendar days after the breach was discovered' (RCW 19.255.010(8))
Notify the Attorney General no more than 30 days after discovery if notification is required to more than 500 Washington residents from a single breach (RCW 19.255.010(7))

Chapter violations are, for AG enforcement purposes, deemed an unfair or deceptive act under the Consumer Protection Act (ch. 19.86 RCW); consumers injured by a violation may bring a civil action, and violators may be enjoined (RCW 19.255.040)
items.notice_deadline: 'most expedient time possible, without unreasonable delay, and no more than thirty calendar days after the breach was discovered'
items.regulator_notice: Washington AG, no more than 30 days after discovery, if notice is required to more than 500 Washington residents from one breach
items.personal_info_definition_notes: RCW 19.255.005(2) includes name + SSN/driver's license or WA ID/financial account or card number with access code/full DOB/private signing key/student, military, or passport ID/health insurance ID/medical or mental-or-physical-condition information/biometric data; also username or email + password or security Q&A permitting account access; and certain data-element combinations without a name if they would enable identity theft.
items.penalties: No fixed statutory civil-penalty amount in RCW 19.255; enforced as a Consumer Protection Act (ch. 19.86 RCW) violation by the AG (parens patriae authority) or via private consumer civil action, with injunctive relief available (RCW 19.255.040); an action under this chapter may not be brought under RCW 19.86.090

items.title: Student User Privacy in Education Rights (SUPER) Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies directly to 'school service providers.' Under RCW 28A.604.030, providers may collect/use/share student personal information only for authorized purposes or with consent, may not sell it, may not use or share it for targeted advertising, and may not build non-authorized student profiles. RCW 28A.604.040 requires a comprehensive information security program and reasonable-time deletion of student data on the educational institution's request.
key_obligations: Collect/use/share student personal information only for purposes authorized by the school/teacher or with consent (RCW 28A.604.030(1))
No sale of student personal information (exception for compliant successor entities on acquisition/merger) (RCW 28A.604.030(2))
No use/sharing of student personal information for targeted advertising (RCW 28A.604.030(3))
No building a personal student profile outside authorized/consented purposes (RCW 28A.604.030(4))
Consent required before materially inconsistent use versus the stated privacy policy/school contract (RCW 28A.604.030(5))
Maintain a comprehensive information security program with administrative, technological, and physical safeguards (RCW 28A.604.040(1))
Delete student personal information within a reasonable time on the educational institution's request, subject to consent/transfer exceptions (RCW 28A.604.040(2))
Subcontractor flow-down: provider may share with a subcontractor only if contractually restricted to the same purposes/nondisclosure/compliance duties (RCW 28A.604.030(6)(f))
items.uncertainty: Chapter-wide enforcement/penalty provision was not independently located this session.

Checked: Washington has never enacted a general CCPA/VCDPA-style comprehensive consumer privacy law. Prior attempts (2019, 2020, 2021) stalled over a private-right-of-action dispute. The current vehicle, HB 1671 'People's Privacy Act,' received a 'do pass' from the House Technology Committee in February 2025 but has sat in the Appropriations Committee without further action through the 2026 session — it has not passed. Washington's only enacted privacy statutes are sectoral: the data breach law (RCW 19.255), the My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373, recorded separately as a health-privacy item), and a biometric privacy statute (RCW 19.375, not separately catalogued here). This finding relies on a secondary summary (recordinglaw.com) rather than a direct fetch of the WA Legislature's bill-tracking page for HB 1671, because the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before an official bill-status page could be located and fetched.

items.title: My Health My Data Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to 'regulated entities' and 'small businesses' that determine the purpose/means of processing consumer health data, and separately regulates 'processors.' Under RCW 19.373.060, a processor may process consumer health data only under a binding contract with the regulated entity/small business that sets processing instructions and limits the processor's actions; a processor acting outside those instructions becomes itself a regulated entity/small business subject to the full chapter for that data.
key_obligations: Maintain and prominently publish (homepage link) a consumer health data privacy policy disclosing categories collected, sources, categories shared, categories of recipients/affiliates, and how consumers exercise rights (RCW 19.373.020)

No collecting or sharing consumer health data without separate, specific consumer consent (or necessity to provide a requested product/service), with detailed consent-disclosure requirements (RCW 19.373.030)
No unlawful discrimination against a consumer for exercising chapter rights (RCW 19.373.030(1)(d))
It is a chapter violation for a regulated entity/small business to contract with a processor in a manner inconsistent with its own consumer health data privacy policy (RCW 19.373.020(1)(e))
Processor must process only per binding contract instructions and assist the regulated entity/small business in meeting chapter obligations (RCW 19.373.060)

Enforced as a per se unfair/deceptive act under the Washington Consumer Protection Act, ch. 19.86 RCW (RCW 19.373.090) — which, unlike most other states' comprehensive privacy statutes, permits a private consumer civil action in addition to AG enforcement
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Consumer health data' covers data used to identify a consumer's past, present, or future physical or mental health status; the Act's scope and consent regime is broader/stricter than most state comprehensive privacy laws' health-data carve-outs.
items.penalties: Enforced via the Consumer Protection Act (ch. 19.86 RCW): treble damages up to $25,000, injunctive relief, and attorney fees are generally available under ch. 19.86 RCW for CPA violations; specific MHMDA penalty text beyond RCW 19.373.090's 'unfair or deceptive act' designation was not independently re-fetched this session.
items.effective_or_amended: 2023 c 191; compliance dates March 31, 2024 (regulated entities) and June 30, 2024 (small businesses)
items.uncertainty: The general ch. 19.86 RCW penalty figures ($25,000 treble-damages cap) are standard CPA remedies, not re-verified against RCW 19.373 text directly this session; RCW 19.373.020 and .030 and .060 and .090 were each individually fetched and confirmed.

items.title: Notice of breach of security of computerized personal information
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §46A-2A-102(c), an individual or entity that maintains computerized data including personal information that it does not own or license shall give notice to the owner or licensee of the information of any breach as soon as practicable following discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed and acquired by an unauthorized person.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify data owner: 'as soon as practicable following discovery' (§46A-2A-102(c))
Owner/licensee must notify affected residents 'without unreasonable delay' following discovery/notification of the breach (§46A-2A-102(a))
If more than 1,000 persons must be notified, also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies without unreasonable delay (§46A-2A-102(f))
No statutory Attorney General pre-notice/threshold requirement found in this article
Failure to comply is an unfair or deceptive act under W. Va. Code § 46A-6-104, enforceable exclusively by the Attorney General absent willful repeated violations (§46A-2A-104)
items.notice_deadline: 'without unreasonable delay' for individual notice; 'as soon as practicable' for vendor-to-owner notice; no fixed day count in the statute
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name linked to unencrypted, unredacted SSN, driver's license/state ID number, or financial account/card number with security code (§46A-2A-101).
items.penalties: AG has exclusive enforcement authority; civil penalty only on a court finding of repeated and willful violations, not to exceed $150,000 per breach or series of similar breaches discovered in a single investigation (§46A-2A-104(b))

items.title: Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act
items.applies_to_vendor: This statute is primarily directed at the West Virginia Department of Education/school districts rather than establishing direct operator prohibitions (unlike SOPIPA-style laws in TX/UT/VT/VA/WA). It binds vendors indirectly: the Department must ensure any contract with a private vendor governing databases, assessments, or instructional supports that include student or redacted data 'include[s] express provisions that safeguard privacy and security and include[s] penalties for noncompliance' (§18-2-5h(c)(6)), and must ensure vendor compliance with a data security plan (encryption, breach planning/notification, retention/disposition policies) (§18-2-5h(c)(4)).
key_obligations: Confidential student information (SSN, religious affiliation, firearm ownership, medical/psychological/behavioral diagnoses, criminal history, biometric data, genetic information, etc., defined at §18-2-5h(b)(11)) may not be transferred to any outside entity except under listed exceptions
Department contracts with vendors for databases/assessments/instructional supports must include express privacy/security safeguards and noncompliance penalties (§18-2-5h(c)(6))

Department must maintain a data security plan covering access authentication, privacy compliance/audits, breach planning and notification, data retention/disposition, and encryption/employee-training safeguards (§18-2-5h(c)(4))
Parents must be notified 'as soon as possible' after a suspected or confirmed data security breach (§18-2-5h(c)(8))
Collection of confidential student information is prohibited outright (§18-2-5h(c)(9))
items.notice_deadline: Parents notified 'as soon as possible' after a suspected or confirmed breach
items.regulator_notice: Governor must be notified upon suspicion or confirmation of a breach, and at regular intervals while it is managed
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Confidential student information' is broadly defined (§18-2-5h(b)(11)) and separately restricted from district-level reporting to the state (§18-2-5h(d)): juvenile delinquency records, criminal records, medical/health records, student biometric information.
items.penalties: Statute requires vendor contracts to include penalties for noncompliance, but does not itself set a statutory penalty amount for vendor violations
items.uncertainty: This is a DOE/school-district-facing statute with a contractual flow-down to vendors, not a direct SOPIPA-style operator-prohibition statute (contrast TX/UT/VT/VA/WA items) — noted so it is not mistaken for the same obligation shape.

Checked: West Virginia has not enacted a comprehensive CCPA/VCDPA-style consumer privacy law. HB 2987 (2025 Consumer Data Protection Act) passed the House 94-1 but died in the Senate Judiciary Committee. HB 5123 (a 2026 reintroduction) also failed to advance before the legislature adjourned sine die March 14, 2026. West Virginia residents rely on the state breach law (W. Va. Code § 46A-2A) plus federal frameworks (HIPAA, GLBA, COPPA, FERPA). This finding relies on a secondary summary rather than a direct fetch of the WV Legislature's official bill-status pages for HB 2987/HB 5123, because the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before those could be located and fetched directly.

items.title: Notice of unauthorized acquisition of personal information
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §134.98(2)(bm), if a person other than an individual that stores personal information pertaining to a Wisconsin resident, but does not own or license it, learns the information has been acquired by an unauthorized person, and has not entered into a contract with the owner/licensee, that person shall notify the owner/licensee of the acquisition as soon as practicable.
key_obligations: In-state entities must make reasonable efforts to notify each affected Wisconsin resident on learning of unauthorized acquisition (§134.98(2)(a))
Out-of-state entities must make reasonable efforts to notify each affected Wisconsin resident (§134.98(2)(b))
Vendor/storer without an owner contract must notify the data owner/licensee 'as soon as practicable' (§134.98(2)(bm))
If notice is required to 1,000+ individuals, also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies without unreasonable delay (§134.98(2)(br))
Notice to individuals must be made 'within a reasonable time, not to exceed 45 days after the entity learns of the acquisition' (§134.98(3)(a))
No Wisconsin Attorney General/DATCP notification requirement is stated in this section
items.notice_deadline: 'within a reasonable time, not to exceed 45 days after the entity learns of the acquisition' (reasonableness considers number of notices required and communication methods available)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Last name + first name/initial linked to unencrypted, unredacted SSN, driver's license/state ID number, financial account/card number with access code, DNA profile, or unique biometric data (fingerprint, voiceprint, retina/iris image, or other unique physical representation) (§134.98(1)(b)).
items.penalties: §134.98(4): failure to comply is not itself negligence or breach of duty, but 'may be evidence of negligence or a breach of a legal duty' — no separate civil-penalty dollar figure is set by this section; no private right of action is created by the statute itself per case-law interpretation reported by a secondary source (not independently re-verified this session)
items.uncertainty: The 'no private right of action' characterization (§134.98(4) commentary) relies on a case-law summary from a secondary source and was not independently verified against appellate case text this session.

Checked: Wisconsin's student-records statute, Wis. Stat. § 118.125 (the Pupil Records Law), restricts school-district access to and disclosure of pupil records but is school/district-facing — it does not, per the sources checked, establish direct operator/vendor prohibitions (targeted advertising ban, data-sale ban, profile-building ban) in the SOPIPA/TSPA style found in TX, UT, VT, VA, and WA. A federated Privacy Compass/FPF tracker of state student-privacy vendor laws did not list a Wisconsin entry. Wisconsin schools remain bound by FERPA. This is a secondary-source-only finding — the WI Legislature's own § 118.125 text was not fetched this session to directly rule out a vendor-facing subsection, and the WebSearch budget was exhausted before a more exhaustive search could be run.

Checked: Wisconsin has not enacted a comprehensive CCPA/VCDPA-style consumer privacy law as of August 2026. Assembly Bill 172 and Senate Bill 166 (2025-26 session) would have created consumer rights to know/opt-out/delete, but both failed to pass on March 23, 2026. Wisconsin relies on targeted statutes (breach notification, record-disposal law). This finding relies on a secondary summary rather than a direct fetch of the WI Legislature's official bill-status pages for AB 172/SB 166, because the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before those could be located and fetched directly.

items.title: Computer security breach; notice to affected persons
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §40-12-502(g), any person who maintains computerized data that includes personal identifying information on behalf of another business entity shall disclose to that business entity any breach of the security of the system as soon as practicable following the determination that the information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person. The maintaining person and the business entity may agree who provides the single required notice; absent agreement, the party with the direct resident relationship must notify.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify the business entity: 'as soon as practicable following the determination' that data was or is believed acquired (§40-12-502(g))

On becoming aware of a breach, conduct a good-faith, reasonable, prompt investigation into likely misuse; if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, give notice 'as soon as possible' to affected Wyoming residents, in the 'most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' (§40-12-502(a))

No statutory Wyoming Attorney General pre-notice/threshold requirement — the AG's role under §40-12-502(f) is enforcement authority (civil action for violations), not a recipient of a mandatory breach notice
Financial institutions and HIPAA-covered entities/business associates that comply with their federal breach regimes are deemed compliant (§40-12-502(c), (h))
items.notice_deadline: 'as soon as possible' / 'most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement' — no fixed day count in the statute
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name combined with one or more data elements specified in Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-901(b)(iii)–(xiv), when not redacted (§40-12-501(a)(vii)); excludes information lawfully available from government records or widely distributed media (§40-12-501(b)).
items.penalties: §40-12-502(f): the Attorney General may bring an action in law or equity to address a violation and recover damages or other appropriate relief; no fixed statutory civil-penalty dollar amount is set for breach-notice violations (the $1,000/violation penalty at §40-12-508 applies only to security-freeze violations, a different part of the same chapter)
items.uncertainty: Source is the official Wyoming Legislature's compiled Title 40 statute PDF (fetched and read directly, §§ 40-12-501–509 confirmed); a per-section permalink on wyoleg.gov was not available/accessible (returned 403) so the full-title compressed-statute PDF is cited instead.

Checked: a Future of Privacy Forum/Student Privacy Compass tracker of state student-data laws that bind vendors/operators lists Wyoming as having only state-level student-data-governance bills (HB0008, HB0009, SF 79) that address state data systems, not vendor-facing restrictions in the SOPIPA/TSPA style. No Wyoming statute equivalent to TX Educ. Code 32.151 / VT 9 V.S.A. 2443a / VA 22.1-289.01 was found. This is a secondary-source-only finding — the Wyoming Legislature's own education title was not independently searched section-by-section this session, and the WebSearch budget was exhausted before a more exhaustive check could be run.

Checked: Wyoming has not enacted a comprehensive CCPA/VCDPA-style consumer privacy law covering private-sector data as of May 2026. A draft Wyoming Data Privacy Act (2024) did not advance; SF0065 (2025) passed the Senate unanimously but failed in the House; SF0020 (signed March 2026) applies only to government entities, not businesses. Wyoming relies on its Consumer Protection Act, the breach-notification statute (Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-501 et seq.), and federal law. This finding relies on a secondary summary rather than a direct fetch of the WY Legislature's official bill-status pages, because the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before those could be located and fetched directly.
